title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire
description: 1911 factory fire in New York City
wiki_lead:
The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire occurred in the Greenwich Village neighborhood of Manhattan, a borough of New York City, on Saturday, March 25, 1911. The fire was the deadliest industrial disaster in the history of the city, and one of the deadliest in U.S. history. The fire caused the deaths of 146 garment workers—123 women and girls and 23 men—who died from either the fire, smoke inhalation, or falling or jumping to their deaths. Most of the victims were recent Italian and Jewish immigrants aged 14 to 23.
The factory was located on the 8th, 9th, and 10th floors of the Asch Building (later the Brown Building), which was built in 1901 and remains standing on the New York University (NYU) campus at 23–29 Washington Place, near Washington Square Park. The building has been designated a National Historic Landmark and a New York City landmark.
Because the doors to the stairwells and exits were locked—a common practice at the time to prevent workers from taking unauthorized breaks and to reduce theft—many of the workers could not escape from the burning building and jumped from the high windows. There were no sprinklers in the building. The fire led to legislation requiring improved factory safety standards and helped spur the growth of the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union (ILGWU), which fought for better working conditions for sweatshop workers.

Background
The Triangle Waist Company factory occupied the 8th, 9th, and 10th floors of the 10-story Asch Building on the northwest corner of Greene Street and Washington Place, just east of Washington Square Park, in the Greenwich Village neighborhood of New York City. Under the ownership of Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, the factory produced women's shirts, known as "shirtwaists". The factory normally employed about 500 workers, mostly young Italian and Jewish immigrant women and girls, who worked nine hours a day on weekdays plus seven hours on Saturdays, earning for their 52 hours of work between $7 and $12 a week, the equivalent of $242 to $415 a week in 2025 currency, or $5.04 to $8.65 per hour. The owners were said to have preferred hiring immigrant women over men because they would work for less and were less likely to unionize against them. Often, these women were poor and young, with little to no education and poor command of English.


Fire

At approximately 4:40 pm on Saturday, March 25, 1911, as the workday was ending, a fire flared up in a scrap bin under one of the cutter's tables at the northeast corner of the 8th floor. The first fire alarm was sent at 4:45 pm; John Gregory, a 24-year-old passerby from East 83rd Street, was the first to spot the blaze from outside, seeing smoke from the upper floor windows as he passed the building. He rushed inside, shouted to an elevator operator that the building was on fire, then jumped into a freight elevator and rode to the tenth floor. grok_lead: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire was an industrial conflagration that engulfed the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors of the Asch Building in New York City's Greenwich Village on March 25, 1911, resulting in the deaths of 146 garment workers at the Triangle Waist Company. The blaze, ignited by sparks on fabric cuttings, spread rapidly through highly flammable materials including piled shirtwaist trimmings and lingered in open bins, consuming the eighth floor within five minutes. Workers, predominantly young immigrant women of Jewish and Italian descent aged in their late teens to early twenties, perished from burns, smoke inhalation, or falls after jumping from ninth-floor windows when escape routes failed. Contributing factors included locked doors intended to deter theft and unauthorized breaks, inward-opening exits that impeded egress amid panicked crowds, a single inadequate fire escape that collapsed under weight, absence of sprinklers or fire alarms, and firefighters' ladders reaching only the sixth floor with nets unable to support fall impacts. Company owners Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, who escaped via the roof, faced manslaughter charges for violating labor laws by maintaining locked doors during work hours but were acquitted by a jury on December 27, 1911, after defense arguments cast reasonable doubt on their direct knowledge of the specific violations. The disaster, the deadliest workplace incident in New York City history, exposed systemic deficiencies in fire safety and building codes, prompting state investigations and legislative reforms including mandatory fire drills, outward-opening doors, and enhanced factory inspections.
